en: Jātaka:
Miscellaneous Section, Chapter on the Rice Field of Śālī Grain.
8. The Mahāmorajātaka:
“If indeed I have been seized by you for the sake of wealth, do not kill me after having captured me alive.”
"Lead me properly into the presence of the king;
I think you will receive wealth of no small kind.
"This [man] is not for your execution today."
The arrow is fixed on the bowstring and the noose is set; I shall release them both,
so that the king of peacocks may go as he pleases.
“He who followed me for seven years,
enduring hunger and thirst day and night—
why then has he now been brought under the power of the snare?”
Do you wish to be released from bondage?
Are you abstaining from taking life without attachment?
Have you granted fearlessness to all living beings?
“Since you wish to release me from this bond, though I have been brought to the power of the snare—
speak to me who abstains from taking life.”
And he who grants fearlessness to all beings—
I ask you, O King of Peacocks, about this matter:
what happiness does he obtain after passing away from here?
“I declare that for one who abstains from taking life and who grants fearlessness to all beings,
there is praise even in this very life.
And he goes to heaven after the breaking up of the body.
“Some say that there are no devas;
they claim that in this very world the soul meets its dissolution.”
Likewise, they speak of the fruit of good and evil deeds,
and of giving as that which has been ordained;
having faith in the words of those Arhats, one should practice accordingly.
"Therefore, I harass the birds.
"Both the moon and the sun, beautiful to behold,
travel across the sky illuminating it;"
“Regarding this world or the next,
how do they speak of them in the world of men?
“The moon and the sun, both beautiful to behold,” [they say].
They travel illuminating the sky;
they belong to the other world and not to this one—
of them it is said in the world of men, "They are devas."
“Right here these inferior doctrines of yours are cast out— those who deny karma,
as well as the fruit of good and evil deeds.”
And those who say that giving is merely "bestowed as a favor":
"Surely this word of yours is true;
for how could a gift ever be without fruit?"
Likewise, how could there be a fruit of good and evil deeds,
and how could that which is ordained as a gift come to be? What should one do, what should one perform, and what should one practice?
"By serving whom, and by what quality of asceticism,
O King of Peacocks, tell me this matter, so that I may not fall into hell."
“Whatever ascetics there are on earth,
clad in saffron robes and living the homeless life,
they wander for alms at the proper time, early in the morning.”
For those who are virtuous and refrain from wandering at improper times,
having approached them there at the right time,
you should ask whatever may be dear to your mind.
They will speak according to their own understanding for the welfare of this world and the next:
"Like a snake casting off its old, worn-out skin,"
Like a tree with pale leaves and green shoots;
this cruelty of mine has been abandoned,
for today I renounce my state as a hunter.
And as for those birds of mine who are bound,
numbering many hundreds in my dwelling,
to them also I give life this very day.
And they have attained liberation, their own true home.
"A hunter wandered through the forest with a snare in hand,
seeking to capture the illustrious lord of peacocks."
“Having bound the illustrious lord of peacocks,
he was released from suffering just as I have been released.
Thus ends the eighth Jātaka, the Mahāmorajātaka.
